sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: arrival order versus driver on the right, the three default speed limits, four seconds versus ten to fifteen seconds versus six to eight seconds
Confusable pairs in the basic control and right-of-way rules, where similar-looking numbers and tie-breakers trip up test takers; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec03-R01 | anchor: A01
At a four-way stop, arrival order decides who goes, and the driver on the right wins only as the tie-breaker when drivers arrive at the same moment. [A01]
Why it matters: group right-of-way; confusable arrival order versus driver on the right.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0013]

FACT_ID: sec03-R02 | anchor: A01
Yielding to the vehicle on your right is the rule for an uncontrolled intersection, but at an uncontrolled T-intersection you yield to the cross traffic. [A01]
Why it matters: group right-of-way; confusable uncontrolled crossroads versus T-intersection.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0013]

FACT_ID: sec03-R03 | anchor: A01
Entering a roundabout, the vehicles you yield to are the ones already circulating inside it. [A01]
Why it matters: group right-of-way; prereq roundabouts; difficulty low.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0013]

FACT_ID: sec03-R04 | anchor: A01
A blind pedestrian with a guide dog or white cane keeps the right-of-way even outside the intersection, and you must stop at least ten feet away until the person clears the road. [A01]
Why it matters: group right-of-way; misconception only in crosswalks.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0013]

FACT_ID: sec03-R05 | anchor: A01
Turning left or making a U-turn, you yield to oncoming vehicles, and you also yield to any vehicle overtaking you on the left or the right. [A01]
Why it matters: group right-of-way; difficulty medium.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0013]

FACT_ID: sec03-R06 | anchor: A02
The residential default is 25 mph unless posted otherwise, the school zone limit with children present is 15 mph, and unposted outlying areas of cities and villages top out at 35 mph. [A02]
Why it matters: group speed limits; confusable twenty-five versus fifteen versus thirty-five.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec03-R07 | anchor: A02
Passing does not permit speeding: you may not exceed the posted limit even briefly to get around another vehicle. [A02]
Why it matters: group speed limits; misconception speeding to pass.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec03-R08 | anchor: A02
Driving too slowly can also earn a ticket and cause crashes, so the safe choice is to match traffic and use the far-right lane when slower. [A02]
Why it matters: group speed; misconception slow is always safe.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec03-R09 | anchor: A02
The acceleration lane is on the on-ramp and is used to speed up, while the deceleration lane is on the off-ramp and is used to slow down. [A02]
Why it matters: group merging; confusable acceleration versus deceleration lane.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec03-R10 | anchor: A02
When merging from an on-ramp, the merging driver is the one responsible for finding a safe gap, even though highway traffic may slow or move over. [A02]
Why it matters: group merging; misconception highway traffic must make room.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec03-R11 | anchor: A02
The four-second count is a following gap, and each adverse condition such as rain, snow, ice or heavier traffic adds one more second. [A02]
Why it matters: group following distance; confusable base count versus added seconds.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0014]

FACT_ID: sec03-R12 | anchor: A03
Seeing 10 to 15 seconds ahead is about how far down the road you look, not about how far behind the next vehicle you follow. [A03]
Why it matters: group visual lead; confusable look-ahead versus following gap.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0015]

FACT_ID: sec03-R13 | anchor: A04
Coasting means rolling in neutral, and the handbook says to stay in gear instead so you keep full control of the vehicle. [A04]
Why it matters: group stopping; misconception neutral is harmless.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0016]

FACT_ID: sec03-R14 | anchor: A04
At a railroad crossing the check is twofold: look and listen for a train, and confirm space for your whole car beyond the tracks before crossing. [A04]
Why it matters: group railroad; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0016]

FACT_ID: sec03-R15 | anchor: A05
Checking the rearview mirror every 6 to 8 seconds is a different number from the four-second following gap, and it is meant to spot tailgaters. [A05]
Why it matters: group space behind; confusable mirror interval versus following gap.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0017]

FACT_ID: sec03-R16 | anchor: A05
The handbook response to a tailgater is a gradual slowdown, which encourages that driver to go around you. [A05]
Why it matters: group space behind; misconception speeding up to escape a tailgater.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0017]

FACT_ID: sec03-R17 | anchor: A05
Stopping on a hill and approaching a railroad crossing are both reasons to leave extra seconds in front, along with following motorcycles or bicycles. [A05]
Why it matters: group space in front; difficulty medium.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0017]
